lead.kicker: Amit Varma argues that nationalism harms every nation
lead.head: Love the country, not the ism
body: The day after India beat Pakistan at cricket, Amit Varma scrolled through Twitter and was deeply disturbed. The players had refused to shake hands. The captain and politicians had made belligerent noises, and social media had erupted after the win.
It made no sense to him. Indian and Pakistani cricketers have always been friendly, he said, and Pakistani commentators such as Wasim Akram are “superbly popular among our people”.

For the common person, Varma argued, nationalism means doing what Doug Stanhope once described: “hating people you have never met and taking pride in accomplishments you had nothing to do with”. {122-S01}

He began by pulling apart three ideas that are often confused. The national interest, he said, is what is good for your country; patriotism is love for your country. Nationalism is “an ideology that I largely tend to think of as kind of toxic”. {122-C01}
His thesis followed: “Nationalism is bad for the nation. Any nationalism, any nation.”
## Strangers in one imagined family

The definition Varma likes best is Benedict Anderson’s: a nation is an imagined political community. Unlike a small tribe, it is made mostly of people we will never meet. “We don’t even know their preferences by and large,” Varma said, “but we imagine it to be something which we define narrowly.” {122-C04}

The tribal instinct beneath it is ancient; the nation is new. Nations are only a few centuries old, yet each claims a glorious past, which has to be invented. The scholar Shruti Kapila, Varma recalled, once called Hindutva “a theory of violence in search of a history”.
In Europe, he said, the printing press, revived vernaculars and the Romantic movement made nations possible. Social media, Varma suspects, is today’s printing press.
## Every good has a twin

Varma granted that nationalism can unite the colonised, bind communities and revive cultures. But every good, he argued, has a matching harm, and the goods can be had in other ways. “You don’t actually need to invent a shared identity to do it.” {122-C09}

His deepest objection is that nationalism, like other identity ideologies, essentialises. “You are tying me down to an identity of birth or location, and you are telling me this is who you are,” he said. That, he argued, dehumanises. {122-C11}

Ajay Shah added that nationalism helps the state, the people’s hired agent, become their ruler. Once you blur the people of Italy and the Italian government, he said, the government “lays claim to the idea that they represent Italy”.
Mussolini, Hitler and Putin, Shah noted, all ended by pouring their own people into war.
## Closer to home

In India, Varma counted three nationalisms born under the British: Hindutva, a Muslim nationalism that became Pakistan, and the secular nationalism of Nehru, Gandhi and Patel. All, he said, are imagined.
The secular idea won, but it was imposed from the top. “People like us failed because we could not do it from the bottom up.”
Nationalism also invades everyday life, Varma argued: language, sport, music, clothes and food. Behind economic nationalism, Shah said, “what’s really going on is just protectionism”.
Varma closed with a plea. Nationalism, he said, diminishes us economically, culturally and in character. “So nationalism is a great diminishment of the self.”
Shah recalled a wish he attributed to Rabindranath Tagore: “the winds from the seven continents to blow through my nation”.

second.label: India and Pakistan
second.head: A mother’s gold medal
second.deck: Amit Varma’s antidote to cricket’s bad blood came from a javelin thrower’s home
body: When Neeraj Chopra won the javelin gold two Olympics ago, Amit Varma recalled, one of the people he praised was Pakistan’s Arshad Nadeem, a close friend whom Neeraj had always encouraged, almost like a mentor.

At the last Olympics it was Arshad who won gold, with what Varma called an outlier throw of “ninety two point something”, and a disappointed Neeraj did not. A TV crew went to Neeraj’s mother to ask how she felt. {#mother} Arshad, she said, was her son too.
That, Varma said, is the sentiment you want between Indians and Pakistanis. “Frankly, we are the same damn people here. It’s the same damn culture.” {122-S07}

quote.text: Because a state will always invoke nationalism to strengthen its own powers and to turn us against each other.

third.head: Full marks for Shudh Hindi
body: In both the 10th and 12th standard, Amit Varma scored more marks in Hindi than in English. He was lazy, he admitted in stronger words, and did not really study. But he had hacked Hindi.

The hack was to learn lots of Shudh Hindi words, dwar instead of darwaza, mitra instead of dost, and string them together. Teachers rewarded it, he said, “because nobody speaks in Shudh Hindi”. {122-S06}

Schoolroom Hindi, Varma argued, was constructed. The north’s living language grew bottom up as a khichdi of influences; then Urdu was painted as Muslim, and a de-Persianised Hindi was consciously promoted. {122-C15}
Imagine English speakers using only Latinate words, he said. Instead of “we shall fight them in the streets”, Winston Churchill would have said “we shall combat them in the boulevards”. {122-J03}

p2.title: Nationalism on trial
p2.deck: Amit Varma’s case that nationalism is bad for the nation, chapter by chapter, with Ajay Shah’s interjections

sections.label: What it is
sections.head: Nobody has met the nation
sections.caption: the imagined community
body: Every nation is imagined, Amit Varma argued. His definition comes from Benedict Anderson’s *Imagined Communities*: a nation is an imagined political community. {122-R01}

The instincts beneath it are ancient. Humans evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes, where solidarity with your own and suspicion of the other were selected for. “And we evolved in those times to be tribalistic.” {122-C03}

The philosopher W. E. H. Lecky described a circle of moral concern that expands over time, from kin to tribe to village. Peter Singer predicted it would one day take in animals. “Alas,” Varma said, “it hasn’t even expanded to include all human beings.”
The nation is one stage of that circle. Unlike a band of Dunbar’s 150, its members are mostly strangers, yet we imagine them as one homogeneous people. {122-C04}
## Three paradoxes

Anderson found three paradoxes in it. Nations are a few centuries old, yet each claims a glorious past. {122-C05} Everyone supposedly has a nationality, yet each is unique. And nationalism is a definite political force that is philosophically nebulous.

There are no great thinkers of nationalism, Varma said. Ajay Shah objected that Mussolini had theory; we are just loath to accept it. Varma replied that Mussolini, Hitler and Savarkar offered assertions, not first principles. “To me you don’t qualify as a serious thinker unless you can tell me the why.” {122-C06}
~ Such men, he said, are men of action, and their worldview is a rationalisation for the terrible things they do.

quote.text: Nationalism is not the awakening of nations to self consciousness. It invents nations where they do not exist.
quote.who: Ernest Gellner, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: How it spread
sections.head: Roses, presses and Pushkin
sections.caption: how nationalism spread
body: In the Europe of the 1300s and 1400s there were no nations, Amit Varma said, only kingdoms, empires and local loyalties, in days before maps or the printing press.

Some historians date English consciousness to the 15th-century Wars of the Roses. The dynastic civil war swept away many feudal overlords, and with them the local allegiance owed to them. Commoners and royals fought side by side and began to feel part of the same people. {122-S02}
Varma deadpanned that *The War of the Roses* was a 1989 film, recently remade as *The Roses*, “but that is completely different”. {122-J02}
## Presses and folk songs

Revived vernaculars such as French and German gave people a common marker, and the printing press gave their stories scale. {#printing} Locke and Rousseau’s will of the people needed a people. The Romantic movement, reacting against a coldly rational Enlightenment, supplied the folk songs and fairy tales.

Russia shows how sticky the thread is. The Tsars used Russification; the communists railed against nationalism; yet at a 1937 celebration of the Soviet Union’s great poets, in Stalin’s time, the Russian Pushkin was feted above all. {122-S04}
~ By the end of the 19th century, he said, nationalism ruled the world. {#rules}

quote.text: One of my theories for the revival and exacerbation of modern nationalism is that social media enables that kind of primitive tribalism

sections.label: Good and bad
sections.head: Every ‘we’ needs a ‘them’
sections.caption: the yin and yang of nationalism
body: Amit Varma gave nationalism its due, then showed the flip side of each good. It can unite the colonised against their rulers, but every oppressor uses it too. The German theorist Carl Schmitt said politics needs an other, and nationalism supplies one automatically. {122-J19}

It can bind people together, but the moment you say we are a Hindu nation or a Muslim nation, someone else is othered. It can revive a culture, but calling one tradition ours declares others not ours.
The goods, he argued, come from elsewhere too: self-government, the economic web of cities, shared tastes such as the cult that follows The Peter Cat Recording Company. {122-R14}
## Love without pride
Ajay Shah cringes at the word pride. Varma loves Van Morrison, Shah pointed out, but is not proud of him. “Pride is something you have got to have done something.” {122-C10}

Worst of all, Varma said, nationalism ties you to an accident of birth and declares it the most important thing about you, baaki sab jaaye bhaad mein. That, he argued, dehumanises: it denies the multitudes each of us contains. {122-C11}
~ Shah added a public-choice view: the people are the principal and the state their agent. Nationalism, he said, has played an important role in the trick that turns citizens into subjects. {122-C12}

quote.text: I contain multitudes, as do all of you.

sections.label: Gone wrong
sections.head: The cauldron of war
sections.caption: nationalism gone wrong
body: Benito Mussolini spelt out the trick himself, Amit Varma said, and read out his words: “It is not the people who make the state, but the state that makes the people.” {122-J20}
Mussolini sold Italians the glories of ancient Rome. Hitler built his nationalism on race, othering a people to the point of genocide and seeking Lebensraum, a Germany expanding into other lands.
Both countries learnt from their mistakes, Varma said. Much of the rest of the world is intent on repeating them.
## Same game, different flag

Communism, with its class war, might seem nationalism’s opposite. But both build an in-group and paint everyone else as the enemy, and Varma traced the Tsars’ Russification through Stalin’s Russia to Putin’s.
For a moment, a better world seemed near: Francis Fukuyama spoke of the end of history, “though you will note with the question mark at the end of the original essay”. {122-R08}
Now even the United States has turned to economic nationalism. It is, Varma said, “like we’re in a bad video game simulation and there’s a bug in the system”. {122-J12}
~ “If only Vladimir Putin could sign on for Rabindranath Tagore as his spiritual guide instead of Alexander Dugin,” Ajay Shah said, “then millions of Russians would be alive today.” {122-J22}

quote.text: What worse destruction of the people could you achieve other than building this cauldron of war and pouring your own people into the war?

sections.label: India’s journey
sections.head: A khichdi, then a cleavage
sections.caption: India’s three nationalisms
body: North India’s language, Amit Varma said, grew “through spontaneous order in this beautiful bottom up way”, a khichdi of Persian, Sanskrit, Prakrit and tongues now dismissed as dialects. {122-C15} A language, as he put it, is a dialect with an army. {122-J26}

Then politics split it. After 1857, he said, the British tried to divide and rule, and movements within both religions pulled apart. Urdu was painted as Muslim, and a de-Persianised Hindi was consciously promoted. Yet the two remain mutually intelligible.
## Three ideas of India

Under the British, three nationalisms grew: a Hindutva aimed more at Muslims than at the British, a Muslim nationalism that became Pakistan, and the secular nationalism of Nehru, Gandhi and Patel. All three, Varma argued, are imagined.

The secular one won, but it was imposed from the top while society, as Akshaya Mukul’s book on the Gita Press shows, held other ideas. Those who shared the secular vision, he said, failed because they could not build it from the bottom up. {122-C14}
Even Ambedkar, Varma noted, called the constitution a mere topsoil. {122-J25}
~ Rabindranath Tagore saw the danger a century ago. He backed Indian independence, Varma said, yet called nationalism “a cruel epidemic of evil eating into humanity’s moral vitality”. {122-J23}

quote.text: The nation, with its flags and pious hymns, cannot hide the fact that the nation is the greatest evil for the earth.
quote.who: Rabindranath Tagore, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: Everyday life
sections.head: Biryani is not anti-national
sections.caption: nationalism in everyday life
body: Nationalism does not stay on maps, Amit Varma said. It invades sport, food, music, clothes and money.
In *The Sporting Spirit*, George Orwell described sport as war minus the shooting. {122-J15}

Varma, a sport lover, backs football teams for their playing philosophy rather than any badge. Ajay Shah, who does not watch sport, proposed random teams with “a little bit of old fashioned capitalism” in the buying and selling of players.

Most of what India eats came from outside, Varma said, so food nationalism is ridiculous. As for the rhetoric about Ajmal Kasab being fed biryani: “Biryani is not anti national,” he said. “I am never going to give up biryani.” {122-J09}
## Pune or Poland

Every voluntary trade is positive-sum, “a double thank you”, Varma said, whether with Pune or Poland. Shah asked what an Indian company even is: about 90 per cent of ICICI Bank’s shareholding is foreign, he said, and Infosys has mostly foreign shareholders and customers. {#icici}

Keeping data on Indian soil means paying for India’s heat, patchy electricity, scarce top-end engineers and tariff-inflated equipment. The data centre should sit in Greenland, Shah said, where the air is cold. {#greenland}
~ Most of the time, Shah said, “the firms want to cry mummy and get a government to support them when they are not able to succeed on their own steam”. {122-C17}

quote.text: Somebody will say data is a new crude oil, which is supposed to be a checkmate.

side.boxText: Benedict Anderson’s *Imagined Communities* is possibly Amit Varma’s favourite book on nationalism. It gave the episode its definition of a nation, an imagined political community, limited and sovereign, and its three paradoxes of nationhood. {122-R01}

contQuote.text: And if we just embrace that and throw ourselves into that and learn from others and listen to their music and learn other languages, our lives are much richer.

p3.title: Accidents of history
p3.deck: Four tales Amit Varma told, from a caliphate to a football war

stories.start: Like when I think of the accidents of history, I think of
stories.end: because Jinnah was a very different man before and after this
stories.caption: Gandhi, Khilafat and Jinnah
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a promise, an alliance and a man’s bitterness
stories.head: Exit the last great moderate
body: Mohandas Gandhi came back from South Africa around 1914, Amit Varma said, and met his great hero, Gopal Krishna Gokhale. {#gandhi1914}
Gokhale found him a bit naive. Do not engage in active politics, he told Gandhi; promise me that for a year you will just travel around India. Gandhi agreed. A month later, Gokhale died.
Gandhi kept his promise anyway, and chose, for some reason, to travel barefoot as a tribute. “I don’t know what the logic of that is,” Varma said, “but he does that.” {122-J13}
At a Congress gathering around 1917 or 1918, nobody took him seriously. He was, in Varma’s words, “this random weird guy who’s come from South Africa”.

His key moment came when he joined the Ali brothers and their Khilafat movement, which wanted the caliphate, abolished at the end of the First World War, revived for the broader Muslim Ummah. Gandhi wanted an independent India. “There’s no coherent reason for them to come together, but they do.” {122-S05}

It proved a tactical masterstroke: around 1920 and 1921, Gandhi took over the Congress. The great moderates of the past had died out, and the last of them, Mohammed Ali Jinnah, thought he would be the next head of the Congress.

Jinnah could not figure Gandhi out. What, he wondered, did Khilafat have to do with an independent India? Embittered, he changed completely, stopped being a moderate and became the biggest proponent of Pakistan.
~ “In a sense the rest is history,” Varma said.
stories.why: Borders and nationalisms that look eternal can turn on accidents: a promise to a mentor who died a month later, an alliance of convenience, one man’s bitterness. Such accidents of history, Varma said, can “lead to crazy consequences”. {#crazy}

stories.start: There's actually a soccer war between Honduras and El Salvador.
stories.end: That is how much uh you know passions can rise because of it
stories.caption: the Soccer War
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a football rivalry that became a war
stories.head: Qualifying for a war
body: In 1969, Amit Varma said, Honduras and El Salvador played a series of qualifying matches for the football World Cup. There was so much sloganeering and fighting during them that a war followed. {122-S08}
As he recalled it, the war lasted 100 days, and six thousand people died. {#soccerwar} It is commonly called the Soccer War.
“It is not that soccer caused the war,” Varma said. “Nationalism caused the war, but soccer was the trigger.”

~ Varma set it beside George Orwell’s essay *The Sporting Spirit*, which, if he remembered correctly, looked at an ugly football match between Glasgow and Moscow, and beside Hitler’s use of the 1936 Berlin Olympics to drive his rhetoric. {#berlin}
stories.why: Sport is tribal, but it does not start these fires; it amplifies passions nationalism has already stoked. In a sense, Varma said, he is happy Pakistan has no great chess players yet: a Gukesh win over a Pakistani would revive the same rhetoric.

stories.start: And you gotta remember that he came in power in the early twenties
stories.end: The people were with him because this was such a popular narrative
stories.caption: Mussolini’s trenchocracy
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how Mussolini sold Italy its lost glory
stories.head: All roads lead to the trenchocracy
body: Benito Mussolini came to power in the early 1920s, Amit Varma said, just after the First World War. He rallied the people by promising that Italy would be ruled by the trenchocracy: the common people who had fought in the war. {#trench}

Mussolini was conveniently located where the Roman Empire had been. Look at the glorious Roman Empire, he told Italians: they were there, we are here, how far we have fallen. {#rome} He spoke of Roman military valour and discipline, and did things with pomp and grandeur.

It worked. All through his disastrous reign, Varma said, Mussolini was supremely popular. “He didn’t even need to be authoritarian in that sense. The people were with him because this was such a popular narrative.” {122-S03}
~ We know the disasters of Italian fascism, Varma said, and where it took Europe.
stories.why: A story of lost glory can do the work of coercion. Promise a people their golden age back, and they may follow a strongman into disaster of their own free will.

stories.start: Like what I am wearing could be called a patan suit
stories.end: clothes have no religion and we are who we are
stories.caption: the religion of clothes
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on clothes, religion and how labels change
stories.head: What’s Muslim about a salwar?
body: What Amit Varma wore for the episode could be called a pathani suit, or a kurta with a Patiala salwar. Is it Muslim or Hindu? “The question is ridiculous,” he said. “Clothes don’t have religion.” {122-S10}
Yet many people, he said, would call his dress Muslim: something worn at Eid, or a sign that you are probably a Muslim. “Which is absolutely terrible.”

When he was growing up in the 1970s and 1980s, salwar kameez was frowned upon even for women, seen as something Muslim women wear. A Kashmiri Pandit, once a close friend, told Varma he did not let his sister wear it. Now, Varma said, it is completely normalised.
~ He reached for an unlikely authority. As Bob Dylan once said, he reminded listeners, even the president of the United States must someday stand naked. {122-J28}
stories.why: Identity politics assigns clothes a faith, and the labels can flip within a generation, as salwar kameez did. Ultimately, Varma said, clothes have no religion and we are who we are.

quiz.q: Which three ideas, often confused, did Amit Varma separate at the start?
quiz.a: The national interest, patriotism and nationalism, which he calls a toxic ideology.

quiz.q: Whose definition of a nation as an imagined political community anchors the episode?
quiz.a: Benedict Anderson’s, from his book *Imagined Communities*, possibly Varma’s favourite on the subject.

quiz.q: Which 15th-century war do some historians credit with the birth of English consciousness?
quiz.a: The Wars of the Roses, which swept away many feudal overlords and local loyalties.

quiz.q: What did Mussolini promise Italians would rule them, after the First World War?
quiz.a: The trenchocracy: the common people who had fought in the war.

quiz.q: Which two countries fought the 1969 Soccer War after a series of World Cup qualifiers?
quiz.a: Honduras and El Salvador; Varma recalls about 100 days and six thousand dead.

quiz.q: Where, according to Ajay Shah, should a data centre serving Indian users sit?
quiz.a: In Greenland, where the air is cold and renewable energy is plentiful.
